title: How One Startup Built a (Mostly) China-Free Robot
gist: After the FCC banned new models of Chinese-made humanoids and other advanced devices on national-security grounds, Ati Robotics CEO Saurabh Chandra details how a Bangalore-based company accidentally built the industry's least China-dependent bill of materials — piggybacking on India's two- and three-wheeler EV component supply chain, choosing induction motors to avoid magnets entirely, and reaching a 10,000-pound tugger where only the battery cells come from China. He names the residual chokepoints (harmonic drives, frameless motors, solid-state lidar, gears) and says the rest of the industry is in denial about the ban after failing to lobby it away.

themes.theme: Regulatory shock and who is exposed

insights.claim: The FCC has banned new models of humanoid robots and other advanced devices from China on national-security grounds, a rule that could hamper growth for many smaller US robotics firms that develop software but source hardware from Chinese suppliers.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on US robotics is now bill-of-materials provenance, not model quality — screen portfolio robotics companies on hardware sourcing before software capability.

insights.claim: Robotics venture investment hit record highs this year in both deal count and dollars per PitchBook, but the capital went disproportionately to software-first companies that still depend on Chinese hardware — a mismatch the ban now exposes.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Peak-funding vintage robotics startups may be structurally mispriced: their capital-light hardware strategy was an asset under free trade and is a liability under the ban.
insights.locator: Investment in robotics startups hit record highs

insights.claim: The industry's response to the ban was denial preceded by failed lobbying — Chandra met people at a conference months earlier who were actively lobbying in Washington to prevent exactly this rule and did not succeed.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Failed lobbying plus industry denial means supply-chain repricing has not yet happened; the adjustment cost is still ahead, not behind.
insights.quote: Everyone’s in denial. Absolutely. It'll get real.
insights.locator: How are people in the robotics industry reacting

insights.claim: The rule is narrower than a blanket component ban — it does not prohibit using any part from China — but Chandra expects quite a few companies to be materially impacted regardless.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: The ban targets finished-model approval rather than parts, so the compliance workaround is assembly and system-level sourcing, not full component decoupling.
insights.quote: The regulation is not saying that you cannot use any part from China.
insights.locator: With this new ban in place

insights.claim: Chandra identifies the beneficiaries as anyone building robots outside China, explicitly naming Tesla's Optimus and US-manufacturing startup Figure alongside European firms, while calling his own company an accidental beneficiary.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: A named beneficiary list from an operator inside the supply chain — Tesla Optimus and Figure are the liquid and near-liquid expressions of the ban's tailwind.
insights.quote: We are an accidental beneficiary. Tesla’s Optimus is obviously a clear beneficiary.
insights.locator: Who do you think will ultimately benefit

insights.claim: Ati financed in-house hardware development by locating R&D in Bangalore and piggybacking on India's two- and three-wheeler EV supply chain, whose components share a similar power profile to robotics drives and are automotive-grade, high-volume and therefore reliable and cost-efficient.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: A reusable playbook: build hardware on top of an adjacent industry's mature volume supply chain rather than a bespoke one — the cost structure comes free with someone else's scale.
insights.locator: R&D is in Bangalore, which helps with our labor costs

insights.claim: The China-independence was a byproduct rather than a strategy: Ati built its own hardware for functional reasons against the advice of many advisers, and that vertical integration naturally limited Chinese reliance.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Vertical hardware integration, widely discouraged as capital-inefficient, is now delivering geopolitical optionality — a reason to re-rate hardware-heavy robotics against software-first peers.

insights.claim: The company pivoted from its 2017 founding purpose of building motors for self-driving cars to building complete robots — tuggers and pallet movers that move tons of material through large facilities — carrying the motor expertise forward as the differentiator.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Motor and actuator competence, not autonomy software, is the transferable asset in this cycle — the same skill that survived the autonomous-vehicle bust now defines robotics defensibility.

insights.claim: Ati's 10,000-pound tugger is described as really China-free with only the battery cells sourced from China, while its pallet mover contains maybe less than 5 percent Chinese parts — a quantified benchmark for how far decoupling can currently go.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Sub-5 percent Chinese content is achievable today in industrial mobile robots, which sets the realistic bar competitors will be measured against under the new rule.
insights.quote: It's really China-free actually. And even the pallet mover has maybe less than 5 percent Chinese parts.
insights.locator: Which of your robots uses the fewest parts from China?

insights.claim: The humanoid remains materially more China-dependent than the industrial robots: the full arm and actuator are built in Bangalore but the harmonic drive, the frameless motor, the gears and the battery cells all still come from China.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Harmonic drives and frameless motors are the humanoid-specific chokepoints — the components to watch for non-Chinese capacity buildout and the ones that will gate Western humanoid production.
insights.locator: But even with the humanoid that we have

insights.claim: Solid-state lidar is a genuine single-source dependency: the pallet mover uses a Chinese solid-state lidar because no option exists outside China, whereas the tugger uses US-based Ouster.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: A clean gap in the non-Chinese supply chain and therefore a specific market opening — non-Chinese solid-state lidar is an unserved demand pocket created by the ban.
insights.locator: In the pallet mover, we use one very good solid-state lidar sensor

insights.claim: Battery cells are characterized as a passive, easily substitutable component — Ati says it could source from South Korea or Japan tomorrow — meaning cell dependency is a price question rather than a strategic vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Distinguish substitutable commodity inputs from true chokepoints when assessing China exposure; cells score far lower on risk than harmonic drives or lidar.
insights.locator: The battery cells come from China

insights.claim: Gears currently sourced from China are also manufactured in Germany, Taiwan and Japan at somewhat higher cost, so the humanoid's supply-chain exposure is a deliberate early-stage cost choice rather than a technical constraint.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Much apparent China dependence in robotics is price-driven and reversible at a modest cost premium — the reshoring transition may be cheaper than headline risk implies.
insights.locator: We don't try to optimize the supply chain from the get-go

insights.claim: Ati uses induction motors specifically so that even the magnet in the motor does not come from China, a design choice Chandra says is very different from what most robotics companies do.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Magnet-free motor architectures are a direct hedge against Chinese rare-earth export controls — a design decision that becomes a valuation input under export restrictions.
insights.quote: We use induction motors, so even the magnet in the motor is not coming from China. That’s a very different choice from many of the people who are doing robots.
insights.locator: There are some components that do come from China

insights.claim: The rare-earth hedge carries a quantifiable engineering penalty: induction motors are slightly less efficient than Chinese brushless magnet motors, but the efficiency loss can be offset with additional battery capacity.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Decoupling from Chinese magnets costs efficiency and weight, not capability — an acceptable trade for stationary-duty industrial robots but a harder one for humanoids and mobile platforms.
insights.quote: you can trade off a bit of efficiency for a bit more battery
insights.locator: Did you have to make some trade-offs?

themes.theme: Commercial traction and where it gets built

insights.claim: Ati has several hundred robots in operation across warehouses and factories with more than 50 customers, and its first humanoid — designed to move heavy bins — enters service later this year.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: Real deployed fleet and revenue base distinguishes this from pre-revenue humanoid narratives; the industrial mobile-robot business funds the humanoid option.
insights.locator: Ati has several hundred robots currently in operation

insights.claim: Supply-chain provenance is not yet an explicit customer buying criterion but many customers have said it influences their decisions — a latent preference the company has not even made central to its marketing.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: China-free sourcing is currently an unpriced tiebreaker that the FCC ban is likely to convert into an explicit procurement requirement — a coming pricing-power shift for compliant vendors.
insights.quote: We have not seen this being a very explicit part of their buying criteria. But many customers have definitely told us that it influences their decisions.
insights.locator: How do you market your robots?

insights.claim: Production is currently entirely in Bangalore but Ati is setting up a facility in Madison Heights near Detroit for eventual US assembly — India as the low-cost manufacturing base with a US final-assembly layer for regulatory access.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: India-build plus US-assemble is the emerging template for accessing the US market under China restrictions; expect the Detroit metro to attract more of this final-assembly capacity.
insights.locator: Where is your humanoid ultimately assembled?

insights.claim: Chandra frames the core problem as an invention-versus-manufacturing gap — most of these robots were invented in the US and it is a tragedy they are not made there — while arguing the barriers to replicating his approach are low.
insights.speaker: Paresh Dave
insights.so_what: If China-free robotics is genuinely replicable rather than proprietary, the ban's beneficiary set widens quickly and first-mover advantage decays — favor incumbents with deployed fleets over sourcing-story startups.
insights.quote: It's not like what we are doing is magic.
insights.locator: Most of these robots have been invented in the US
